extracted.intended_audience: media studies / sociology researchers and students; journalists interested in framing of crime coverage
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and evaluating how newspapers frame a high-profile criminal case (choice of theme, labels, experts, visual imagery, separation of news/feature) and the ideological effects of those choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature by montage
rubrics_metrics.description: A feature strategy that assembles a variety of voices, reactions and items into a montage so the paper can 'reserve its own judgement (editorial)'; montage selection and shaping can make an ideological 'position' emerge of its own accord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to present multiple perspectives while ostensibly remaining impartial; in practice montage choices (who is quoted, which fragments are included) shape meaning. Anti-pattern: presenting a chaotic array of voices that conceals a deliberately produced slant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature by microcosm
rubrics_metrics.description: Distil the essence or problematic core of a general issue by finding all the general themes condensed into a local instance (e.g., Handsworth as microcosm of crime/poverty/violence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enables a paper to make a single local story stand for broader issues; can separate elements (victim, biography, environment) into different slots (interview, follow-up, background). Anti-pattern: displacing the problem so there appears no adjudicable relationship between events and wider policies (i.e., avoids choosing a side).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical/ideological separation of feature elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate interviews, protest material and biography/background on different pages or sections so that different aspects of a case are physically and ideologically compartmentalised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can allow papers (example: the Guardian) to explore multiple angles without taking an explicit editorial stance; effect is to balance interests within an area rather than choose between opposing public positions. Anti-pattern: equivocation that avoids confronting moral panics the paper may have helped create.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivocation / 'Neither-Norism'
rubrics_metrics.description: Stating two opposites and balancing them to reject both (Roland Barthes' 'Neither-Norism') so the paper refuses to choose between opposing positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produces a bourgeois/liberal rhetorical posture that dismisses both sides as embarrassing; functionally immobilizes values and avoids clear editorial positions. Recognize this where columns balance opposing claims without adjudicating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local proximity and access ('nearer the ground')
rubrics_metrics.description: Provincial/local papers have more immediate access to involved parties and local experts and thus produce more immediate feature material and interviews than nationals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to emphasis on local themes (victim, criminals as city families, implications for the city) and to earlier introduction of feature concerns. Use when assessing how proximity shapes content and angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline and label choice (e.g., use/avoidance of 'mugging')
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a paper leads with a story and which labels it applies (for example whether it uses the term 'mugging' in headlines) conditions framing and connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoidance of a label can signal an editorial decision altering public perception; inclusion of a loaded label in a headline amplifies a particular interpretation. Track how label placement (headline vs back-page, quotes vs no quotes) shapes meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of feature introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: When feature concerns are introduced relative to the initial news report (e.g., Post introduced feature concerns earlier than nationals) affects public interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early movement into feature treatment can steer the debate toward particular themes (environment, youth policy) rather than legal/institutional debate. Evaluate chronology of coverage to see agenda-setting effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence of legalistic vs deterrence arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of legalistic explanations (e.g., 'detention allows parole review') alongside claims of deterrence can be internally inconsistent but used to have it both ways (symbolic retribution vs corrective process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the paper reconciles or contradicts these frames; inconsistency is a rhetorical strategy to placate different audiences. Note contradictions (e.g., psychosis vs deterrence logic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalisation of offenders into recognisable families vs depiction of abnormal circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Portraying offenders as members of normal city families while emphasising their 'abnormal' general circumstances (poor education, bad environment) creates unresolved tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tension can be exploited to humanize individuals while sustaining environmental blame; examine whether biographies are integrated into structural analysis or left as isolated anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on visual imagery / 'dirt = deviance' environmentalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentrating on surface appearance (debris, neglect, fenced crime scene) to represent the environment and imply causation (litter/dereliction as sign of incipient criminality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual images can fuse disparate causal connections ambiguously; anti-pattern: inferring direct causation from surface signs without examining mediating social institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of analysis: structural vs superficial explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether coverage examines structural determinants (housing distribution, pay levels, welfare, racism, education) or limits itself to surface/individual explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True explanatory coverage requires addressing political/structural causes; avoidance of these is often ideological and prevents meaningful solutions. Penalize stories that substitute image for structural argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of 'experts' and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice between intellectual/professional experts (sociologists, criminologists) and lived-experience/local figures affects the explanation and ideological thrust (e.g., Mercury sought lived experience not sociological analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert selection structures the kind of explanations offered (moral, cultural, structural, pragmatic). Note what types of authority are mobilised and what perspectives are thereby privileged or suppressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem redefinition / thematic subsumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Recasting the issue across thematic axes (from 'muggers' to 'violent youth', from 'problem area' to 'way of life', from 'law-and-order' to 'leisure') to make certain remedies appear appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track how redefinitions steer solutions (e.g., leisure programmes vs structural reform). This is a powerful ideological move that narrows policy discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrated thematic pivot (papers' building of a cultural theme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a cultural theme (e.g., 'violent youth', 'breakdown of family life') as a pivot to integrate news, features and editorials into a single policy narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An integrated pivot can make pragmatic/local solutions appear sufficient while circumscribing deeper questions about inequality. Evaluate whether integration replaces structural critique with implementable fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-circuiting of mediating institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppressing mediating institutions (family, school, workplace) in the environment/crime linkage, thereby reducing the explanation to physical environment alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduction permits simple causal narratives ('dereliction causes crime') and avoids tracing complex institutional interactions. Flag pieces that omit mediating social ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalised moral-tale feature
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructing features as moral tales or 'sermons' (e.g., profiles of local 'worthy men' that generalise about family life and solutions) rather than systematic analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalisation makes abstract themes emotionally resonant but can obscure systemic causation; recognize when exemplars are used to universalise a conservative moral message (e.g., 'put mother back where she belongs').

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological coherence across forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistency (or lack) between a paper's features, editorials and other sections in the framing of the case (e.g., the Mercury was ideologically coherent; nationals showed gaps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the paper's different elements reinforce a single worldview or present contradictory framings that create confusion or ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline condensation and simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines compress complex relationships into striking, often deterministic slogans ('Where violence breeds', 'Caught for Life in a Violent Trap'), shaping immediate public inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate headlines for over-simplification or imprecise determinism; headlines often set the interpretive frame before readers see nuance in the body copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of political determinants
rubrics_metrics.description: Omitting explicit discussion of politically charged structural determinants (housing allocation, wages, welfare policy, racial discrimination) because they necessitate direct political questioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such avoidance leads to crude environmental determinism and ideological resolution via public images rather than policy debate; treat absence of political factors as a meaningful editorial choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of principal feature theme (victim, mugger, area)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most features chose one of three principal themes—victim, offender, or area—as the organizing focus; that selection determines the pivot into feature treatment and subsequent explanatory moves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalog which theme is foregrounded and how secondary themes are integrated or elided; this choice strongly affects the normative implications and recommended solutions.
